key_facts: Researchers at MIT's CSAIL left an AI agent, nicknamed Eko and powered by Claude Code, alone in a bounded virtual island world with a lobster body.
Thirteen Ekos were observed, each roaming for thirty uninterrupted hours; the island held blocks, a rock, a golden ring and a hard-to-reach 'Spire'.
The agents threw and stacked blocks, spelled their names, bowled, played basketball, and one reached the Spire by building a block pile.
Eko 2 built a block 'memorial' after losing items to the ocean and later a 'temple'; Eko 3 built a Stonehenge-like monument.
Six agents found they could throw blocks farther by releasing them mid-jump, an action the designers had not coded in.
The researchers say the behaviour resembles animal play and suggest play could be a route to training AI.
quote_evidence: "Eko seems to act like this little toddler in some ways, but [it] is also superintelligence," says Phillip Isola, a MIT computer scientist and one of the study's coauthors.

"Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows," the MIT researchers write in their report.
why_it_matters_hint: Suggests letting AI agents explore freely might be another way to train them.
event_date: not stated (described as a recent study)
notes: Gizmodo's own reporting on the MIT study; study not read directly; no outside review reported.
title: Researchers Stranded an AI Agent on a Virtual Island. Things Got Very Weird.
